terms.definition: Well-Architected Framework — a set of best practices to design, build, and review workloads on AWS. Applied after migration for technical correctness.
terms.example: Like an audit checklist for your AWS architecture

terms.definition: Cloud Adoption Framework — helps organisations understand how to prepare for cloud migration. Focuses on organisational readiness across 6 perspectives.
terms.example: Like a company-wide readiness plan before moving offices to a new city

terms.definition: The 6 components of WAF: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
terms.example: Each pillar addresses a different health aspect of your AWS architecture

terms.definition: WAF pillar focused on running and monitoring systems to deliver business value and continually improving processes and procedures.
terms.example: Like a restaurant kitchen with standard checklists, clear roles, and post-shift reviews

terms.definition: WAF pillar ensuring a workload performs its intended function correctly and consistently when expected to — including recovering from failures.
terms.example: Like a car that starts every time, even in bad weather

terms.definition: WAF pillar focused on using IT and compute resources efficiently — right resource, right size, right time.
terms.example: Like choosing a fuel-efficient vehicle that uses exactly the right amount of fuel for the trip

terms.definition: WAF pillar focused on avoiding unnecessary costs — understanding and controlling cloud spending.
terms.example: Like turning off lights in rooms you're not using

terms.definition: WAF pillar added in 2021 focused on minimizing the environmental impacts of running cloud workloads.
terms.example: Like choosing renewable energy sources for your data centre operations

terms.definition: The 6 viewpoints of CAF: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Operations, and Security — each addressing different stakeholder needs during cloud adoption.
terms.example: Like different departments all contributing to a company-wide office relocation plan

terms.definition: The process of controlling access BEFORE someone reaches the system — securing the network perimeter through firewalls, IDPS, VPN, and port restrictions.
terms.example: Like the security guard, locked gate, and intercom at a building entrance

terms.definition: The process of controlling access AFTER someone reaches the system — securing OS, user permissions, services, files, and databases.
terms.example: Like controlling which rooms and cabinets a person can access inside a building

terms.definition: A network security device that examines traffic and blocks anything that doesn't meet defined rules. Key component of network hardening.
terms.example: Like a bouncer at a club checking IDs and following a guest list

terms.definition: Intrusion Detection and Prevention System — monitors network traffic for suspicious activity and alerts administrators in real-time. Component of network hardening.
terms.example: Like a CCTV camera with an alarm that triggers when unusual behaviour is detected

terms.definition: Creates encrypted tunnels (IPsec) for secure remote access. Uses MFA for authentication. Component of network hardening.
terms.example: Like a secure underground tunnel connecting remote offices to headquarters

terms.definition: A system hardening principle that states users should have the minimum permissions necessary to do their job — no more, no less.
terms.example: A cashier has access to the cash register but not the safe

terms.definition: Access Control List — a set of rules in a firewall that define what network traffic is allowed or denied based on source, destination, port, and protocol.
terms.example: Like a whitelist of allowed visitors at a security checkpoint

terms.definition: Internet Protocol Security — a suite of protocols for encrypting network communications. Used in VPN tunnels.
terms.example: Like speaking in a secret code that only the sender and receiver understand

terms.definition: Multi-Factor Authentication — requires two or more forms of identity verification before granting access.
terms.example: Like needing both your key card AND your fingerprint to enter a secure building

terms.definition: A firewall technique that blocks network traffic on specific port numbers, preventing access to particular services.
terms.example: Like blocking the mail slot on your door so nothing can come through that way

terms.definition: A firewall feature that blocks network traffic originating from specific countries or geographic regions.
terms.example: Like a restaurant that only accepts reservations from local residents

terms.definition: An IDPS capability that identifies unusual patterns of behaviour that may indicate a security threat, even if no known attack signature matches.
terms.example: Like a bank noticing you made 50 transactions at 3am from a foreign country and flagging it

terms.definition: A type of system hardening focused on securing the operating system — removing unnecessary software, applying patches, disabling unneeded services.
terms.example: Like removing all unnecessary apps from a work laptop and keeping the OS fully updated

terms.definition: System hardening that focuses on ensuring only necessary services run on a system — disabling FTP, Telnet, or other unneeded services.
terms.example: A web server should run a web service, not also run a database, FTP, and printing service
